title: Maximum Manhattan Partition Factor
statement:
A city is modelled as a 2-D plane with houses built at `n` points. For two points `(x1, y1)` and `(x2, y2)`, the Manhattan distance between them is `|x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|`.

Divide the `n` points into two groups so that each point belongs to exactly one group and **each group contains at least one point**. The **partition factor** of a partition is the minimum Manhattan distance over all pairs of different points that lie in the **same** group.

Given the points, return the maximum partition factor that can be achieved over all valid ways of splitting them into two groups. Because `n ≥ 3`, at least one group always contains a pair of points, so the factor is always defined.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines contains two integers `x` and `y`: the coordinates of a point.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the maximum possible partition factor.

examples.explanation: Splitting into { (0,0), (3,3) } and { (2,2) } gives a single same-group pair at distance 6. The other two splits give factors 4 and 2, so the maximum is 6.

The pairs (1,1)-(1,2) and (5,5)-(5,6) are at distance 1, so each pair must be split across the groups. Taking { (1,1), (5,5) } and { (1,2), (5,6) } gives same-group distances 8 and 8, so the factor is 8, and the other valid splits are worse.

hints: For a target `d`, any two points closer than `d` must go into different groups. When can such a split exist?
Think of points as vertices and 'closer than d' pairs as edges: a valid split exists exactly when this graph is bipartite. As `d` grows, edges are only added.
Build a minimum spanning tree of the complete graph (Prim in O(n^2)) and 2-colour it. The answer is the smallest distance between two distinct points of the same colour.
